ranges.heading: Stop distance follows the invalidation question

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: The source suggests wider stops for reversals and smaller stops for trends. Neither relationship is universal. If a wider stop is justified by the setup, sizing must be reconsidered within the same loss budget; do not increase quantity or stop distance merely to recover a loss.

ranges.heading: Hit rate, reward-to-risk and entry timing

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: A high win rate can coexist with negative expectancy, and a large planned reward-to-risk ratio can coexist with frequent losses. Approximate net expectancy is win probability × average win − loss probability × average loss − average costs. A later entry changes both distance to invalidation and remaining target distance; neither risk direction nor profitability follows from early/late alone.

editorialSections.heading: Sizing from a stated loss budget
paragraphs: For a simple linear instrument, divide a hypothetical cash risk budget by estimated loss per unit at the stop, including a defensible allowance for per-unit costs. Then round down to the permitted quantity and check contract, tick/pip and account-currency conversions. Nonlinear instruments require scenario-based valuation instead.

Arithmetic example only: a 50-unit cash budget and 12-unit estimated loss per contract allow at most four whole contracts under those assumptions. A worse fill, changed conversion rate or gap can exceed that estimate. Margin required to open a position is a separate number.

A stop triggers when a threshold is reached and can then execute at a different price, depending on the order/product. The source associates limits with reversals and stops with breakouts; those are strategy examples, not the definitions of the orders. Waiting for a bar close changes timing but does not prove a signal.

ranges.heading: VAR, VARMA, BVAR and ARIMA are models, not chart overlays

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: VAR models interdependencies among lagged multivariate series. VARMA adds moving-average error dynamics; it does not automatically remove overfitting. BVAR uses Bayesian priors, whose choice matters. ARIMA models differencing/autoregressive/moving-average structure. Select complexity and assess stability and forecast performance using time-respecting validation.

references.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice — vector autoregressions

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: The name refers to a limit-order-book market-making model associated with inventory-sensitive quotes. It is not a generic directional indicator. The underlying assumptions and estimated order arrival/fill behavior matter; a reference to the model supplies neither a runnable strategy nor a profit guarantee.

references.title: Avellaneda and Stoikov: High-frequency trading in a limit order book

ranges.heading: Price processes, option pricing, allocation and volatility
ranges.introduction: GBM is a continuous-path model and does not include jumps by construction. BSM concerns model-based European-option valuation, not a promise of the actual market price. Mean–variance allocation depends on unstable estimated inputs and constraints. GARCH describes conditional variance dynamics, not certainty about future volatility.

ranges.heading: Dependence, hidden states, dimensions and growth
ranges.introduction: Cointegration concerns stationary combinations under a specified model, not guaranteed profitable convergence. HMM state labels are model interpretations. PCA is an unsupervised transformation, not evidence of economic causality. Kelly sizing depends critically on the assumed outcome distribution and can produce substantial drawdowns.

ranges.heading: Tail dependence, learning, regression and simulation
ranges.introduction: Copulas separate dependence modelling from marginal distributions; tail behavior requires evidence. Neural networks and regressions need leakage controls and unseen-data evaluation. Monte Carlo produces scenarios from its chosen model, not all possible market paths. Factor and Kalman models depend on definitions and state/noise assumptions.

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: A hypothesis test assesses compatibility with a specified null model; it does not determine that a trading pattern is real or exclude luck. Multiple trials, dependence and strategy selection change interpretation. A stationarity test cannot certify that a market process will stay stable; distinguish null hypotheses, deterministic terms, power and structural changes.

references.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice — vector autoregressions

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: Portfolio constraints limit stated exposures under the model; they do not eliminate losses. VaR is a model/distribution quantile for a specified horizon, confidence and position definition, and can be exceeded. Expected shortfall describes average loss in the worst specified tail; for continuous distributions it can be expressed as a conditional tail average. Neither is a guaranteed maximum loss, and discrete tail definitions need care.

ranges.heading: Transaction costs, impact and performance
ranges.introduction: Distinguish fixed commissions, spreads, financing, slippage and size-dependent impact. Market impact is one component of trading friction and should not be double-counted. Compare net returns, drawdowns and uncertainty under a reproducible accounting convention.

title: Trading discipline: planning, practice and an evidence-based journal
summary: Connect the training notes on consistency, mistakes, greed and collaboration to decisions you can review.
takeaway: A disciplined process makes behavior reviewable; repeatability alone does not make an unprofitable rule profitable.

review.status: Reviewed explanation; original training notes retained
paragraphs: The source assigns mindset 60%, money 30% and method 10%. No measurement or study supports those weights here. Small-account results may not scale because liquidity, impact, leverage, operations and behavior change. The cautions about chasing, revenge trading, averaging down and premature exits belong in a defined plan; neither feeling committed nor following a plan guarantees a favorable outcome.

ranges.heading: Five mistake themes
ranges.introduction: Keep the five source themes: weak planning, inadequate practice, psychology, greed/complacency and isolation. Collaboration can reveal errors but can also spread groupthink; practice and gradual scaling still need outcome evidence.

editorialSections.heading: A journal that separates process from outcome
paragraphs: Before a trade or simulation, record the rule version, context, trigger, invalidation, planned size and exits. Afterward, record actual fills, costs, changes and rule deviations. Review winning rule violations and losing compliant trades separately so a lucky outcome does not certify the decision.
Evaluate a series of observations with uncertainty and market context. A single loss does not automatically invalidate a rule, and a short winning run does not establish skill.

title: Behavioral biases: 41 prompts for reviewing trading decisions
summary: Explore the full source bias list, with clarified meanings and practical review questions.
takeaway: Use these concepts to examine a decision process, not to diagnose a person or explain every market move after the fact.

references.title: Nobel Prize: scientific background on decision making under uncertainty

visuals.title: Beliefs, ownership and updating
rows: Overconfidence bias
Overstate the accuracy of a judgement or estimate.
Record uncertainty and compare forecasts with outcomes.
Endowment bias
Value something more because you hold or regard it as yours.
Reassess the position using the same criteria as a fresh decision.
Conservatism bias
Update beliefs too little when relevant evidence changes.
State what evidence would change the view.
Regret aversion bias
Avoid a decision because of anticipated regret.
Assess alternatives and their risks, including doing nothing.
Loss aversion bias
Evaluate losses and equivalent gains asymmetrically relative to a reference point; a fixed twice-as-large effect is not universal.
Inspect how the reference point changes the choice.
Cognitive dissonance bias
Discomfort from conflicting beliefs/actions may encourage rationalization.
Write down disconfirming evidence before explaining it away.
Representativeness bias
Judge by resemblance while neglecting base rates or sample size.
Compare base rates and the amount of evidence.
Confirmation bias
Favor evidence consistent with an existing view.
Search for an observation that would contradict it.
Hindsight bias
Treat an observed outcome as having been more predictable than it was.
Preserve timestamped reasoning before the result.
Self-attribution bias
Attribute favorable outcomes to skill and unfavorable ones to external causes.
Apply the same attribution criteria to wins and losses.
Optimism bias
Underestimate adverse outcomes or overestimate favorable ones.
Use adverse scenarios as well as the preferred case.
visuals.note: Concepts overlap; their presence does not by itself establish the cause of a particular outcome.

visuals.title: Groups, samples and accessible information
rows: Herd instinct bias
Follow a group rather than independently assess the evidence; it is not limited to fear.
Separate observed consensus from reasons.
Hometown bias
Prefer familiar or local exposures; the source label is kept distinct from a precise measured home-bias statistic.
Check concentration and omitted alternatives.
Recency bias
Give disproportionate weight to recent observations.
Compare the recent window with a justified longer sample.
Survivorship bias
Assess only entities/strategies that remain visible or survive.
Include failures, delistings and discarded trials where relevant.
Backfill bias
Historical performance added after selection may favor successful records.
Distinguish contemporaneously available data from later additions.
Anchoring bias
Let an initial value influence later judgement too strongly.
Re-estimate from current evidence without the original number.
Availability bias
Overweight information that is easy to recall or imagine.
Compare vivid examples with representative data.
Action bias
Favor taking action even when inaction may be appropriate.
Require an explicit decision condition.
Omission bias
Judge harmful inaction differently from an equivalent harmful action.
Evaluate consequences of both action and inaction.
Self-serving bias
Interpret events in ways favorable to oneself; overlaps with self-attribution.
Use consistent external review criteria.
Self-selection bias
People who opt into a sample may differ systematically from those who do not.
Inspect recruitment and missing participants.
Association bias
A broad source label for influence through association; no precise mechanism is supplied.
Separate association, evidence and causal explanation.
In-group Out-group bias
Evaluate people or ideas differently according to perceived group membership.
Apply the same evidential criteria across sources.
visuals.note: Concepts overlap; their presence does not by itself establish the cause of a particular outcome.

visuals.title: Observation, defaults and probability
rows: Information bias
The source wording is ambiguous; in decision-making it can mean seeking information that does not improve the decision, while research uses the term differently.
Ask which decision-relevant uncertainty the information resolves.
Observer bias
Expectations can influence what is recorded or interpreted.
Define observations consistently and check independent records.
Status-quo bias
Prefer the current/default state because it is the status quo.
Compare the default with alternatives on equal terms.
Liking bias
Favor a person or proposal because of personal liking.
Evaluate the claim separately from the person.
Blind-spot bias
Notice biases in others while overlooking one’s own.
Apply the same checklist to your own reasoning.
Narrative fallacy
Prefer a coherent story over an adequate account of uncertainty and alternatives.
Record competing explanations and omitted evidence.
Gambler’s fallacy
Assume a run changes the next outcome probability when trials are independent.
State the dependence model; past losses do not create a debt owed by chance.
Conjunction fallacy
Judge a combined event more likely than one of its component events.
Check that an intersection cannot exceed either component probability.
Sunk cost fallacy
Let irrecoverable past costs justify a future commitment.
Compare future costs and benefits from the current point.
Planning fallacy
Underestimate time, effort or cost despite relevant past experience.
Compare with outcomes from similar prior tasks.

visuals.title: Control, perception and social explanation
rows: Illusion of control
Overestimate personal influence over an outcome.
Separate controllable actions from market outcomes.
Müller–Lyer illusion
An optical length illusion, not a trading-performance mechanism.
Measure rather than infer length from surrounding shapes.
Source credibility
Judgements about expertise and trustworthiness; this is not automatically a bias.
Check the underlying evidence, incentives and domain expertise.
Repetition effect
Repeated exposure may increase familiarity or perceived truth without new evidence.
Count independent evidence rather than repeated copies.
Prospect theory
A framework for reference-dependent choice under risk, including nonlinear probability weighting and gain/loss valuation; not simply having more options.
Inspect framing, reference points and how probabilities are weighted.
Groupthink
Pressure for agreement can suppress critical assessment or dissent.
Invite an independent alternative explanation.
Pareidolia
Perceive a familiar pattern in ambiguous or random input.
Specify recognition criteria before assessing later outcomes.

editorialSections.heading: A minimum reproducible strategy specification
paragraphs: Specify instrument/feed, timezone, bar construction, calculation/settings, entry timing, invalidation, quantity, costs and exit conditions. Record which ambiguities remain. Keep parameter development separate from evaluation on later or otherwise genuinely unseen data.

Paper/replay results are conditional simulations. Check look-ahead, survivorship, repeated strategy/parameter trials, data revisions, financing, bid–ask execution, slippage and missed/partial fills. Report net outcomes, drawdowns and uncertainty rather than only the best chart examples.

editorialSections.heading: Resource purposes and boundaries
paragraphs: A position-size calculator needs contract/account inputs; an event calendar needs date/timezone and confirmation against the issuing body. Currency-strength views depend on normalization and lookback. A portfolio allocation backtest is not a tick-level execution simulator for a short-term FX strategy.
